newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens mark independence declaration anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Chechens mark independence declaration anniversary.

text.p: Thousands of Chechens on Friday celebrated the fifth anniversary of their declared independence and what they they hope is the end of a bitter 21-month conflict with Russia.
Many gathered in this tiny village southeast of the Chechen capital Grozny where a shrine to independence fighters stands, and greeted separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev as the guest of honour.
"Today, we are remembering the dead and wounded in this war," Yandarbiyev, in camouflage uniform and traditional lambswool "papkha" hat, told the crowd.
Surrounded by Chechen fighters, he was hustled back to his car as the huge crowd pressed in to hug him and shake his hand.

The peace agreement signed last Saturday between Kremlin envoy Alexander Lebed and Chechen military commander Aslan Maskhadov has halted fighting which began in December 1994 when Russian troops entered Chechnya to crush an independence bid.

But the fear of renewed violence was evident in the crowd as a loud explosion in the distance caused many to jump. They were reassured that it was only the Russians destroying mines as part of the Lebed-brokered peace deal.
"Today is like a party after a funeral, a holiday, not a victory celebration," said Saidem Aadayev, fresh from slaughtering two cows for the feast that lay ahead, his hands still bloody.
"In every village and town, people are celebrating," he added, wiping sweat from his forehead as the sun blazed down.
People milled around the dusty graves of those who fell during the war, next to a shrine to Chechens who had fought for independence in 1919.
"There are so many graves. How can this be called a victory?" said Zelimkhan Uonusov.

All around people danced in circles, singing traditional Chechen songs and chanting prayers. In a field opposite the shrine, men stood in rows facing Mecca in prayer, and heard the preachings of a warrior-like mullah dressed in a green robe and green beret and wearing sunglasses.
The cows slaughtered earlier were sliced on a huge chopping block and chunks of meat were boiled with potatoes in cauldrons. People queued for large portions of steaming stew.
The agreement between Lebed and Maskhadov postponed a decision on independence for five years. Many Chechens said they were happy with this.

"We are peaceful people. We did not want this war," said Isa Dzhankhayev, who said he had recently buried two victims of the war. "We want an independent state but now we are ready for compromise," he added.
The atmosphere was relaxed and festive, with tooting car horns, people shouting "Allahu Akbar" (God is the Greatest) and waving the green flags of Ichkeria, as Chechens call their land.
But the person everyone wanted to be there was absent -- former rebel leader Dzhokhar Dudayev, reported killed in a rocket attack in April.
Many Chechens refuse to accept that he died -- his body has never been seen publicly -- and carried placards with his portrait, believing that one day he will reappear.
"Dudayev will stay in the hearts and minds of all our people..We do not doubt that he is alive," said Sultan Mustiyev.
